title: Delaware's tidal wetlands
creator: NASA Earth Observatory images by Michala Garrison, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey. Story by Kathryn Hansen.
credit: NASA Earth Observatory images by Michala Garrison, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey. Story by Kathryn Hansen. · Public domain
modifications: Resized to a maximum 960 px and JPEG-compressed. Display cropping only; no generated content, recoloring, or retouching.
alt: A Landsat view of green tidal marshes, branching waterways, and land near Dover, Delaware.
reason: A local landscape grounds ecosystem study. This natural-color satellite image is not a ground-level photograph or food-web diagram.
provenance: NASA Earth Observatory's documented Landsat image, acquired September 3, 2024; uses USGS data.
sourceDescription: In the low-lying reaches of Delaware, the land breathes with the ebb and flow of the tide. These tides support the marshes (tidal wetlands) lining much of Delaware Bay. Marshes are one of several wetland types that together cover about one-quarter of Delaware—the second-smallest U.S. state. These semi-aquatic ecosystems, which provide habitat for plants and animals, improve water quality, and help protect against flooding and erosion. These images, acquired on September 3, 2024, with the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 8, show a segment of the region’s coastal wetlands in Delaware and New Jersey. In the false-color image (right), open water appears dark blue, and low-lying areas inundated with water (marsh) appear dark blue-green. Farther inland, the vegetation in agricultural, forested, and urban areas appears bright green. Tidal wetlands lie at the intersection of land and water, where the shore meets an ocean, bay, river, or stream. They regularly flood and drain with the rise and fall of the tides. When these images were acquired at about 11:40 a.m. local time (15:40 Uni

sourceDescription: The Horse in Motion by Eadweard Muybridge . Noted photographer, Eadweard Muybridge was hired, in 1872, by Leland Stanford a railroad baron and future university founder, to find out if there was moment mid-stride where horses had all hooves off the ground. It took several years but Muybridge delivered having captured a horse, named "Sallie Gardner," owned by Stanford ; running at a 1:40 gait over the Palo Alto track, on 19th June 1878. Muybridge used a dozen cameras all triggered one after another with a set of strings.

title: A mathematical instrument
creator: User:Kolossos
modifications: Resized to a maximum 960 px and JPEG-compressed. Display cropping only; no generated content, recoloring, or retouching.
alt: The brass stepped-drum mechanism of Leibniz's mechanical calculating machine.

provenance: User Kolossos's photograph of the documented stepped reckoner; source record predates contemporary generative imagery.
sourceDescription: The Staffelwalze, or Stepped Reckoner , a digital calculating machine invented by Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz around 1672 and built around 1700, on display in the Technische Sammlungen museum in Dresden, Germany. It was the first known calculator that could perform all four arithmetic operations; addition, subtraction, multiplication and division. 67 cm (26 inches) long. The cover plate of the rear section is off to show the wheels of the 16 digit accumulator. Only two machines were made. The single surviving prototype is in the National Library of Lower Saxony (Niedersächsische Landesbibliothek) in Hannover ; this is a contemporary replica.

title: Words shaped for an audience
creator: Abraham Lincoln
modifications: Resized to a maximum 960 px and JPEG-compressed. Display cropping only; no generated content, recoloring, or retouching.
alt: Abraham Lincoln's handwritten Bliss copy of the Gettysburg Address.
reason: Lincoln's handwritten address provides a real example of authored rhetoric. It is not the fictional school-board passage used in the module.
provenance: Abraham Lincoln's final draft of the address, written in March 1864, as documented by its archival source.
sourceDescription: Lincoln's fifth and final draft of the Gettysburg Address, written in March 1864 as a favor for a friend to help raise funds for the Union cause. Because of the apparent care in its preparation, and in part because Lincoln provided a title and signed and dated this copy, it has become the standard version of the address and the source for most facsimile reproductions of Lincoln's Gettysburg Address. It is the version that is inscribed on the South wall of the Lincoln Memorial. This copy is kept on view in the Lincoln Bedroom on the second floor of the White House.
